questions.stem: Lymphocytes respond to antigens. Which description of an antigen is correct?
options: A white blood cell that engulfs pathogens by phagocytosis
A drug that kills bacteria by attacking their cell walls
A molecule, usually a protein, that triggers an immune response
A protein made by plasma cells that binds to and disables a pathogen
questions.explanation: Antigens are molecules, usually proteins or glycoproteins on the surface of pathogens or cells, that trigger a specific immune response. The proteins that bind them are antibodies.

questions.stem: Where do B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes mature?
options: Both B and T cells mature in the lymph nodes
Both B and T cells mature in the spleen
B cells in the bone marrow; T cells in the thymus
B cells in the thymus; T cells in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: Both types of lymphocyte are produced in the bone marrow. B cells mature there, while T cells travel to the thymus to mature. Mature lymphocytes then gather in lymph nodes, the spleen and other lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: Why does each B lymphocyte respond to only one antigen?
options: Its receptors fit the shape of only one antigen
It contains only one gene, which codes for every antibody
It can travel to only one part of the body in the lymph
It is made in a gland that produces one antibody at a time
questions.explanation: Each B cell carries receptors of one shape on its membrane. Only an antigen that fits these receptors can activate that B cell, which is why the response is specific.

questions.stem: What does it mean for the immune system to distinguish self from non-self?
options: Phagocytes engulf only those cells that carry antibodies on them
Antibodies are made against the body's cells until they are replaced
Lymphocytes recognise the body's own markers and leave them alone
Lymphocytes attack every cell that does not contain a nucleus
questions.explanation: Body cells carry their own marker proteins (MHC markers). Lymphocytes that would react against these self markers are normally removed during development, so the immune system targets only foreign antigens.

questions.stem: What is the role of an antigen-presenting cell, such as a macrophage, in the specific immune response?
options: It secretes large quantities of antibodies into the blood and lymph
It kills body cells infected by viruses by punching holes in them
It remembers the antigen for many years so the response is faster
It engulfs a pathogen and shows its antigens to helper T cells
questions.explanation: After engulfing a pathogen, a macrophage or dendritic cell displays fragments of its antigens on its surface. Helper T cells with matching receptors recognise these and become activated, starting the specific response.

questions.stem: Which cells secrete antibodies?
options: Macrophages, which develop from monocytes
Memory T cells, which develop from helper T cells
Plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes
Cytotoxic T cells, which develop in the thymus
questions.explanation: When a B cell is activated, it divides to form a clone. Many of the cells become plasma cells, which secrete large amounts of antibody, and some become memory B cells.

questions.stem: Which sequence best describes the humoral response to a new bacterial antigen?
options: B cell engulfs bacterium, it divides, cytotoxic T cells secrete antibodies into the blood
B cell binds antigen, helper T cells activate it, it divides, plasma cells secrete antibodies
Plasma cells bind antigen, they divide, helper T cells secrete antibodies, B cells form memory
Helper T cells secrete antibodies, B cells divide, plasma cells engulf the bacteria directly
questions.explanation: A B cell with matching receptors binds the antigen and, with signals from helper T cells, divides rapidly (clonal expansion). The clone forms plasma cells that secrete antibodies and memory cells that remain.

questions.stem: What part of an antibody binds to the antigen?
options: The constant region at the base of its stem
The hinge region where the two arms meet
The heavy chains only, along their whole length
The variable regions at the tips of the arms
questions.explanation: The variable regions at the ends of the arms have a shape that differs between antibodies and is complementary to one antigen. The constant region is the same within a class of antibody and interacts with other parts of the immune system.

questions.stem: Antibodies bind to bacteria and clump them together. How does this help the body?
options: Clumped bacteria release heat, which triggers a fever in the host
Clumped bacteria form memory cells that protect against reinfection
Clumped bacteria are dissolved directly by the antibodies themselves
Clumped bacteria are easier for phagocytes to engulf
questions.explanation: This clumping, called agglutination, immobilises the bacteria and makes them easier targets for phagocytes. Antibodies also neutralise toxins and viruses and mark pathogens for destruction, but they do not dissolve bacteria themselves.

questions.stem: Antibodies can bind to viruses in the blood, but they have little effect once a virus is inside a body cell. Why?
options: Antibodies act outside cells; infected cells are killed by T cells
Antibodies are broken down by the virus as soon as they reach the infected cell
Antibodies can bind only to bacteria, so viruses are dealt with by fever instead
Antibodies enter the infected cell but cannot find the virus within the nucleus
questions.explanation: Antibodies act in body fluids, such as blood and lymph, and can stop viruses entering cells. Once a virus is inside a cell, the cell-mediated response is needed: cytotoxic T cells recognise and kill the infected cell.

questions.stem: What is the role of cytotoxic (killer) T cells?
options: To secrete antibodies that circulate in the blood
To engulf bacteria and digest them in vacuoles
To release histamine that causes inflammation
To destroy infected or cancerous body cells
questions.explanation: Cytotoxic T cells recognise foreign antigens displayed on infected or abnormal body cells and kill those cells, for example by releasing proteins that make holes in their membranes.

questions.stem: Helper T cells are often described as central to the specific immune response. Why?
options: They directly kill infected cells by binding to their antigens
They release signals that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells
They are the only cells able to engulf and digest pathogens in the body
They secrete antibodies of every type into the blood and lymph
questions.explanation: Activated helper T cells release cytokines that stimulate B cells to divide and form plasma cells and that activate cytotoxic T cells. Without them, both arms of the specific response are weakened.

questions.stem: HIV infects and destroys helper T cells. Why does this leave people vulnerable to many different infections?
options: Without them, both antibody and cell-mediated responses weaken
Without helper T cells, the skin and mucous membranes stop acting as barriers
Without helper T cells, phagocytes multiply out of control and damage tissues
Without helper T cells, the body produces antibodies against its own cells only
questions.explanation: Helper T cells activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells. As HIV destroys them, the body's specific responses to all kinds of pathogens decline, so infections that a healthy immune system would control can become serious.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares humoral and cell-mediated immunity?
options: Humoral immunity acts through T cells; cell-mediated immunity acts through antibodies in body fluids
Humoral immunity is non-specific; cell-mediated immunity is specific and produces memory cells
Humoral immunity targets infected body cells; cell-mediated immunity targets free bacteria only
Humoral immunity acts through antibodies in body fluids; cell-mediated immunity acts through T cells
questions.explanation: The humoral response is carried out by antibodies from B cells, which act on pathogens and toxins in blood and lymph. The cell-mediated response is carried out by T cells, which act directly on infected or abnormal cells. Both are specific.

questions.stem: A transplanted kidney is rejected some weeks after surgery. Which part of the immune response is mainly responsible?
options: Fever raising body temperature until the donor cells are destroyed
Cytotoxic T cells recognising the donor's cell markers as foreign
Histamine from mast cells causing the kidney to swell and burst
Lysozyme in the blood breaking down the cell walls of the kidney
questions.explanation: The donor's cells carry MHC markers that differ from the recipient's, so T cells recognise them as non-self and attack the organ. Matching donor and recipient markers and using immunosuppressive drugs reduces rejection.

questions.stem: After an infection is cleared, some lymphocytes persist as memory cells. What do they do?
options: They store antibodies made earlier and release them all at once
They carry information about pathogens from the brain to lymph nodes
They persist and respond rapidly if the same antigen returns
They engulf pathogens and remember where in the body they were found
questions.explanation: Memory B and T cells are long-lived cells produced during the first response to an antigen. On re-exposure they divide quickly, producing a faster and larger response.

questions.stem: How does the secondary immune response differ from the primary response?
options: It is the same speed but produces no memory cells
It is faster but relies only on non-specific defences
It is faster and produces more antibodies for longer
It is slower but produces antibodies of a stronger kind
questions.explanation: Because memory cells are already present, the secondary response begins sooner, reaches a much higher antibody concentration and lasts longer. Often the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms appear.

questions.stem: A graph shows antibody levels after two exposures to the same antigen, 40 days apart. After the first exposure, antibodies peak at a low level about 10 days later. After the second, they rise within 2 to 3 days to a level about 10 times higher. What accounts for the difference?
options: Memory cells formed in the first response divide rapidly on the second exposure
Antibodies left from the first response bind the antigen and multiply themselves
The antigen is weaker on the second exposure, so it is cleared more easily
Non-specific defences learn from the first exposure and act more strongly
questions.explanation: The first exposure produced memory B cells. When the antigen returns, these cells quickly form plasma cells, giving a faster, larger response. Antibodies are proteins and cannot multiply, and non-specific defences do not have memory.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between active and passive immunity?
options: Active: lasts only weeks; passive: lasts a lifetime because memory cells form
Active: the body makes its own antibodies; passive: antibodies are received from elsewhere
Active: antibodies are received from elsewhere; passive: the body makes its own antibodies
Active: given by injection; passive: caught from the environment naturally
questions.explanation: In active immunity the person's own lymphocytes respond to an antigen, producing antibodies and memory cells. In passive immunity ready-made antibodies are received, so no memory cells form and protection is short-lived.

questions.stem: A newborn baby is protected against some diseases for a few months. Which type of immunity is this, and how was it gained?
options: Artificial passive immunity, from antibodies given just after birth
Artificial active immunity, from vaccines given to the mother in labour
Natural passive immunity, from antibodies that crossed the placenta
Natural active immunity, from memory cells passed through the placenta
questions.explanation: Some of the mother's antibodies cross the placenta into the fetus. These provide protection after birth, but they are gradually broken down and the baby makes no memory cells, so the protection fades.

questions.stem: A bushwalker bitten by a venomous snake is given antivenom, which contains antibodies against the venom. Why is this treatment used instead of a vaccine?
options: The antibodies are cheaper to produce than vaccines and can be stored for longer
The antibodies act at once; a vaccine takes days or weeks to protect
The antibodies produce memory cells, so the walker will be protected for life
The antibodies stimulate the walker's own B cells to make a faster response
questions.explanation: Antibody serum gives artificial passive immunity, which works straight away, and that is essential for venom. A vaccine would give active immunity only after the immune system had time to respond. Antivenom produces no memory cells.

questions.stem: A person catches chickenpox as a child and does not catch it again. Which type of immunity do they have?
options: Artificial passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
questions.explanation: The person's own immune system responded to the virus after natural exposure, producing antibodies and memory cells. Active immunity gained through infection is natural; through a vaccine it is artificial.

questions.stem: Breast milk, especially the first milk, contains antibodies from the mother. What type of immunity does a breastfed baby gain from them?
options: Artificial active immunity
Natural passive immunity
Natural active immunity
Artificial passive immunity
questions.explanation: The baby receives ready-made antibodies by a natural route, so the immunity is natural and passive. The baby's own lymphocytes have not responded, so no memory cells form and the protection is temporary.

questions.stem: Why does passive immunity protect for only a short time, while active immunity can last for years?
options: Received antibodies are stronger and wear out the immune system
Received antibodies attack the body's own cells after a few weeks
Received antibodies stop the body ever making its own antibodies
Received antibodies are broken down and no memory cells are formed
questions.explanation: Antibodies are proteins that are gradually broken down. In passive immunity the person's lymphocytes have not responded, so there are no memory cells to make more antibodies when the antigen appears again.

questions.stem: How does a vaccine produce immunity?
options: It supplies ready-made antibodies that remain in the blood for the rest of life
It kills any pathogens already in the body before they can begin to multiply
It strengthens the skin and mucous membranes so pathogens cannot enter
It exposes the body to antigens so memory cells form without disease
questions.explanation: A vaccine contains antigens from a pathogen, in a form that does not cause the disease. The immune system responds by making antibodies and memory cells, giving artificial active immunity.

questions.stem: What is an attenuated vaccine?
options: One containing a live pathogen weakened so it does not cause disease
One containing pathogens killed by heat or chemicals before injection
One containing antibodies collected from a person who has recovered
One containing a toxin that has been made more powerful in the laboratory
questions.explanation: Attenuated vaccines contain living pathogens that have been weakened, so they can still multiply a little and trigger a strong response without causing disease. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine is an example.

questions.stem: The tetanus vaccine contains the tetanus toxin, chemically treated so that it is harmless but still carries its antigens. What type of vaccine is this?
options: A live attenuated vaccine
An antibody serum
A whole-cell killed vaccine
A toxoid vaccine
questions.explanation: A toxoid is an inactivated toxin. It stimulates antibodies that neutralise the real toxin, which is useful against bacteria such as Clostridium tetani that cause disease mainly through their toxins. An antibody serum gives passive, not active, immunity.

questions.stem: Why are booster doses of some vaccines needed?
options: They replace the antibodies destroyed by the first dose of the vaccine
They change the vaccine into a passive form that works more quickly
They kill memory cells formed by the first dose, which were faulty
They restimulate memory cells, raising antibody levels again
questions.explanation: A booster produces a secondary response, which gives a larger rise in antibodies and more memory cells. For some vaccines, protection fades over time unless it is boosted.

questions.stem: Live attenuated vaccines are usually not given to people whose immune systems are severely weakened. Why?
options: The vaccine would cause their immune system to stop working altogether
The weakened pathogen might multiply enough to cause disease in them
The vaccine contains antibodies that would attack their remaining cells
Their bodies would produce too many memory cells and become damaged
questions.explanation: In a healthy person the immune system easily controls the weakened pathogen. In someone with a weakened immune system it may multiply and cause illness, so inactivated or subunit vaccines are used where possible.

questions.stem: Why does high vaccination coverage protect people in a community who cannot be vaccinated?
options: The pathogen becomes attenuated after passing through vaccinated people
Vaccinated people produce memory cells that enter the bodies of others
Few people can catch or spread the pathogen, so it seldom reaches them
Vaccinated people pass their antibodies to unvaccinated people nearby
questions.explanation: When most people are immune, chains of transmission are broken, so the pathogen cannot spread easily. This herd immunity protects babies too young to vaccinate and people who cannot be vaccinated for medical reasons.

questions.stem: How is the hepatitis B vaccine made using recombinant DNA technology?
options: Human genes for antibodies are put into the virus so that it cannot infect cells
A viral surface protein gene is put into yeast, which makes the protein
The whole hepatitis B virus is grown in yeast and then weakened with chemicals
Antibodies to hepatitis B are taken from recovered patients and purified
questions.explanation: The gene for a hepatitis B surface antigen is inserted into yeast cells, which make large amounts of the protein. The purified protein is the vaccine, so it contains no virus and cannot cause infection.

questions.stem: What is a key safety advantage of a recombinant subunit vaccine compared with a live attenuated vaccine?
options: It contains the entire viral genome, so it gives a broader response
It contains only an antigen protein, so it cannot cause the disease
It contains ready-made antibodies, so it gives protection immediately
It contains more live pathogen, so fewer doses are ever required
questions.explanation: A recombinant subunit vaccine contains only a protein made from a pathogen gene, with no pathogen that could multiply. This makes it safe for people who should avoid live vaccines, though boosters may be needed for strong protection.

questions.stem: The human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine contains virus-like particles made of viral coat protein produced by genetically modified cells. Why can it not cause an HPV infection?
options: The particles stay in the muscle and never meet any immune cells
The particles contain no viral DNA, so they cannot replicate
The particles contain antibodies that destroy any HPV they encounter
The particles are made from killed bacteria rather than from a virus
questions.explanation: The coat proteins assemble into particles that look like the virus to the immune system, so they stimulate a strong response, but with no viral DNA inside they cannot infect cells or replicate.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an economic factor influencing a family's decision to immunise a child?
options: Whether the family's religious community accepts or rejects vaccination
Whether friends and neighbours have shared stories about vaccine side effects
Whether the family trusts the information given by health professionals
Whether the vaccine is free, and the cost of travelling to a clinic
questions.explanation: Economic factors involve money and resources: the cost of the vaccine, transport and time off work. Religious beliefs are cultural factors, and the views of friends and trust in information are social factors.

questions.stem: Which is a cultural factor that might influence a person's decision about immunisation?
options: The cost of the vaccine if it is not publicly funded
Religious or traditional beliefs about medicine
The distance from home to the nearest health clinic
Government payments linked to a child's immunisation
questions.explanation: Cultural factors include religious beliefs, traditions and language. Distance and cost are economic or access factors, and government payments are an economic incentive.

questions.stem: In a community, rumours about vaccine side effects spread on social media and vaccination rates fall. A measles outbreak then occurs. Which statement best explains the link?
options: The rumours changed the measles virus, making it resistant to the vaccine
Unvaccinated people passed on their memory cells, spreading the virus further
Herd immunity weakened, so the virus could spread among unvaccinated people
The vaccine had caused the measles outbreak among those who were vaccinated
questions.explanation: Measles is highly contagious, so a high proportion of people must be immune to stop it spreading. When coverage drops, the virus can pass between susceptible people. This is a social factor influencing decisions and so affecting public health.

questions.stem: A government links some family payments to children being up to date with their vaccinations. What is this policy mainly trying to do?
options: Make vaccines give passive rather than active immunity
Reduce the number of doses each vaccine schedule needs
Use an economic incentive to raise vaccination coverage
Use a cultural tradition to raise vaccination coverage
questions.explanation: Linking payments to immunisation status uses an economic incentive to encourage families to vaccinate. Policies like this can increase coverage, though they also raise debate about personal choice.
